title: Vowels Game in a String
statement:
Two players, Alice and Bob, alternate turns on the string `s`, and Alice moves first. On each of her turns Alice must delete one non-empty substring (a contiguous block of characters) that holds an **odd** number of vowels; on each of his turns Bob must delete one non-empty substring that holds an **even** number of vowels, where zero counts as even. After a deletion the remaining parts join up and play continues on the shorter string. A player who has no legal deletion when it is their turn loses.

Assuming both sides play perfectly, return `true` when Alice is the winner and `false` when Bob is. Only `a`, `e`, `i`, `o` and `u` are vowels.
constraints: s consists only of lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Searching the game tree over every string that can remain is exponential, but Alice's first move already decides the game:

- **No vowels.** Every substring holds zero vowels, an even number, so Alice has no legal deletion and loses at once.
- **An odd number of vowels.** Alice deletes the whole string, and Bob faces an empty string with nothing to delete.
- **An even, positive number of vowels.** Alice deletes a piece holding all the vowels but the last one (an odd count), for example everything before the last vowel. Any piece Bob might take that contains the lone vowel holds exactly one vowel, which is odd, so that vowel survives his turn (if it is all that is left, he cannot move at all). On her next turn the string holds exactly one vowel, so Alice deletes all of it and Bob is stuck.

So Alice wins exactly when `s` contains at least one vowel; the parity of the count never changes the outcome.

## Approach

1. Put the five vowels in the set `vowels` and start `count` at 0.
2. Walk through `s`; whenever `ch` is a vowel, add one to `count`.
3. Return `count > 0`. (Stopping at the first vowel works too; the full count keeps the case analysis visible.)

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "leetcoder"` holds the vowels `e`, `e`, `o`, `e`, so `count` ends at 4. That is even but positive, so the answer is `true`. One winning line: Alice deletes `"leetco"` (3 vowels) and leaves `"der"`; Bob can only delete consonants, say `"d"`; Alice deletes `"er"` and Bob has no move.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), one pass over `s`.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Returning `count % 2 === 1` is the classic wrong answer: an even, nonzero count is still a win for Alice.
- Zero is even, so Bob can always delete a consonant-only piece when one exists; the argument works because he can never delete the last vowel.
- Only `a`, `e`, `i`, `o` and `u` are vowels; `y` is not.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `vowels` | the set of the five vowel letters |
| `count` | how many vowels `s` contains |
| `ch` | the character being examined |

narration.2: Put the five vowels in a set so each character can be checked quickly.
narration.3: count will hold the number of vowels in s.
narration.4: Look at every character of the string once.
narration.5: Is this character one of a, e, i, o, u?
narration.9: No vowels means Alice cannot move; an odd count lets her delete everything, and an even nonzero count lets her leave a single vowel Bob can never delete, so any vowel at all means Alice wins.
